profile.intro: M.Arch student at North Dakota State University.

projects.title: The Neighborhood That Owns Itself
projects.text:
How can architecture, backed by a community ownership model, turn underused urban land into affordable mixed-use neighborhoods that reinvest in themselves without displacing the people already there?

The thesis pairs a community land trust with infill and adaptive reuse across a Detroit block, keeping housing, productive space and local enterprise affordable while preserving the identity of the neighborhood. Drawings and design development are on the way.

projects.title: the ROOK
projects.text:
A mixed-use senior housing community in downtown Bismarck, designed so residents can age in place and grounded in the Bismarck 2045 Comprehensive Plan.

A U-shaped plan wraps a central Green Corridor. A concrete podium carries mass timber above, and the building targets LEED Platinum through passive solar design, stack-effect ventilation and photovoltaic generation.

projects.title: Sanford Physical Therapy Clinic
projects.text:
A clinic that brings Sanford's Fargo physical therapy locations under one roof, with aquatic therapy, gym therapy, analytic spaces, private rooms and a smoothie shop in the lobby.

The building sits into earth mounds that engage the site, add room for mobility testing and block street noise. Three-story atria light the main circulation, and a light-filtering skin brings daylight to patient spaces while keeping them private. Biophilia, proportion and natural light led every decision.

projects.title: Ellipses & Ink Bookstore
projects.text:
A semester's worth of detailing and construction in one project. The building sits just off the downtown corridor in Fargo, and the design itself takes a back seat to the drawings.

The work covers wall details, interior elevations, sections, site and schedules, and ends as a 42-page construction set.

projects.title: Teal Prairie
projects.team: Team of six, architecture and landscape architecture
projects.text:
A plaza outside NDSU's Renaissance Hall in downtown Fargo that ties the school to the Avery Apartments opening in 2026. The name and design come from the landscape around it.

Teal points to the nearby Red River, which inspired an interactive pebble pit. Prairie refers to the tall grasses echoed in the pavilion and the movable wind breaks, which keep the plaza changing. Grass mounds with live trees meet concrete forms with sculptural trees, leaving room for both creativity and quiet as well as spaces for winter and summer use.

projects.title: C O N T I N U U M
projects.text:
A pavilion for EXPO 2025 in Osaka, designed to teach about and inspire movement around connecting generations.

True to the theme, the structure is meant to be reused, not recycled. The client, a wood tycoon from northern Minnesota, asked for a stick and timber structural system that still answers to its site.

projects.title: LOCAVORE
projects.text:
A farmers' market and flexible public space on the river in Moorhead. A new public ramp down to the river's edge brings major accessibility improvements to downtown.

The building is raised above the flood line, since flooding is frequent here. Garage doors open the market up in warm months and keep it usable through the cold ones.

projects.title: PELLA Windows & Doors
projects.text:
A competition entry for a new PELLA showroom in Fargo. The brief called for a distinctive structure that uses passive design efficiently and features PELLA products.

The passive systems are blended into the structure itself, for a welcoming, brand-centered building. More detail on the passive systems is available on request.

projects.title: Radiant Pathways Cultural Center
projects.text:
A cultural center in Santa Fe's Railyard District, one of the few places in the city where buildings can explore materials beyond adobe.

The studio traveled to Santa Fe to interview residents and immerse ourselves in the site. The brief pushed into masonry and into designing for a climate and context very different from the Midwest.

projects.title: NDSU Museum & Archives
projects.text:
A museum and archive that extends NDSU's downtown campus and invites the public in.

The large building respects the setbacks and geometry around it while opening up with big windows and spaces of refuge. A two-story opening and grand staircase are meant to inspire visitors as they arrive.

projects.title: Personal Project
projects.text:
A city built continuously for more than ten years, driven not by assignments but by genuine interest in architecture, urban space and systems.

Buildings are designed around facade, scale, material logic and context. Neighborhoods are planned around circulation, density, landmarks and spatial hierarchy.

research.title: The Neighborhood That Owns Itself
research.course: M.Arch Thesis, advised by Professor Charlott Greub
research.summary: Transforming underinvested urban areas into affordable mixed-use housing, supported by a community ownership model, in Detroit, Michigan.
questions: Community ownership: how a community land trust can keep a neighborhood affordable and let it reinvest in itself.
Urban design: how infill and adaptive reuse across a Detroit block can add housing, productive space and local enterprise while keeping the neighborhood's identity.
Together: how the ownership model and the design strategy can work as one, so growth happens without displacing the existing community.

research.title: Between the Folds
research.course: ARCH 474, NDSU School of Design, Architecture and Art
research.summary: How can building typologies from very different regions live together in one neighborhood? Eleven paper models, folded on site in eleven European cities, test that question through observation, materiality and lived experience rather than formal planning. Visitors can rearrange the models into their own neighborhoods, because there is no single ideal city.
cities: Prefabricated postwar apartment blocks with shared courtyards
A light-filled Scandinavian modern museum linking art and nature
A medieval and baroque hotel where locals and travelers meet
A church as neighborhood landmark and gathering place
A mill tied to water and natural systems
A train station linking residents to the wider world
A cafe and theater for performance and conversation
A town hall as a symbol of civic order and access
A school for knowledge exchange across generations
A restaurant where dining is a cultural art form
A hospital that heals through calm and nature
research.methods: Each model was folded and painted while standing in its city, in paper chosen for its forgiving, human quality. Walking, listening and conversations with locals shaped the work, alongside attention to scale, material, movement and how people actually used each space.
research.refs: Jan Gehl, Life Between Buildings and Cities for People. Jane Jacobs, The Death and Life of Great American Cities. Carlos Moreno, the 15-Minute City. SPACE10, The Ideal City.

about.text:
I'm an architecture student and emerging professional with experience in CAD drafting, 3D modeling and architectural visioning, built through school and two years interning at Holland Basham Architects in Omaha.

I also lead. As Student Body Vice President at NDSU, I managed a $4.2 million budget and worked with the North Dakota Legislature on drafting policy, alongside Greek life and the School of Design, Architecture and Art.

I'm drawn to adaptable, thoughtful spaces that respond to present needs and future change, with clarity, flexibility and intent. Collaboration, clear communication and continual learning guide how I work.
